A benevolent and cautious authority. In the late 1340s and early 1350s, Mr. Karbaschi was one of the distinguished students of the late Mr. Shobeiri. According to what I have heard, Ayatollah Shobeiri was cautious in both jurisprudence and politics — the very principle that traditional Shia scholars regarded as a sign of piety. Caution means examining a matter from all sides before expressing an opinion or taking action — in other words, never wading into water without first finding a crossing — which is precisely what some clerics claiming revolutionary fervor have completely abandoned and cast aside! A cautious authority is extremely watchful of his tongue and his actions, is not one for controversy, does not level accusations against others, and for this reason is usually silent or very taciturn. The late Mr. Shobeiri, in addition to this, was inclined toward tolerance and benevolence in political matters. Although he did not speak of it, in practice he would act to the best of his ability to redress injustice or to free from political entanglement those he knew closely. In 1397, the presence of the late Ayatollah Shobeiri at the home of Sheikh Abdullah Nouri, along with the presence of Seyyed Mohammad Khatami, provoked the anger of Sheikh Mohammad Yazdi in his capacity as "Secretary of the Supreme Council of the Seminary"! Ayatollah Shobeiri, in accordance with his conduct, showed no reaction to Mr. Yazdi's behavior and remained silent — a silence that was full of things said and unsaid. At the same time, Hassan Rahimpour Azghadi also accused traditional seminarians of promoting secularism and deemed them secular themselves. Mr. Azghadi's reference was apparently to people like the late Mr. Shobeiri, who did not act and did not speak according to his "revolutionary preferences"! entry.title:
[ahmadzeidabad] Unipolar and multipolar!
Has the world order ever been unipolar? Some call the…
entry.summary:
Machine-translated from the original Telegram post.

Source: @ahmadzeidabad

Unipolar and multipolar!

Has the world order ever been unipolar? Some call the order of the years following the collapse of the Soviet Union unipolar, but the reality is otherwise. In my view, the world has never seen a unipolar order and never will!

Is the world now heading toward a multipolar order? In my view, a "multipolar order" is the most dangerous possible state for the world, because it is not order at all — it is the very essence of disorder and instability! The emergence of a hypothetical multipolar situation in the world would mean the end of our world through devastating wars waged with weapons of mass destruction! When we speak of a "pole," the conflict of interests is its most important defining feature. The conflict of interests ultimately leads to war, leaving destruction and annihilation in its wake. If, to avoid war, a mechanism for resolving disputes were defined, then in its light the very concept of a pole would fade — because a dispute-resolution mechanism is nothing other than the definition and pursuit of common interests, and once common interests come into play, the pole loses its conventional meaning.

Today we are faced with a world in which every member plays a role proportionate to its own capacity. No member is uncontested, and no member is without influence.

A combination of the types and degrees of influence of approximately 200 members of the international community shapes the order of today's world. An infinitely intricate network, grounded in deep mutual interdependence among the members of the global community, has taken shape — one that renders obsolete all the traditional concepts customary in the international system.

We Iranians, whatever our political and ideological leanings, seem in our subconscious to be influenced by bipolar thinking — or rather by the dualistic worldview of our ancestors — and for this very reason we not only welcome polarization but are incapable of observing and understanding the world and its affairs except through its lens!

This outlook has darkened our view of reality and has cost us dearly.

As Rumi said:

Before your eyes you held a blue glass;
for that reason the world appeared blue to you.

I will explain more on this matter.

#احمد_زیدآبادی
@ahmadzeidabad

In truth, the late Taleghani was indeed of a different kind. The resonance of his clear voice in the environment of the University of Tehran acted like the blowing of a pleasant and gentle breeze upon hearts fearful and anxious about the fire of the power-seeking conflicts of the age. His voice was full of a spiritual freshness yet accompanied by much sorrow, warning, and deep concern about the future. It was as if he knew what lay ahead. He knew well many of his peers and the various political organizations of that day, and he knew precisely what goal each of them was pursuing behind their pompous and hollow slogans. He did not enter into the game of any of them, nor did he consent to the elimination and exclusion of any of them. He tried to offer a rule for the coexistence of all of them within a pluralist framework, but it was as if he knew how the story would unfold! He concealed his suffering, sorrow, distress, dissatisfaction, and desperation, but it seemed that the poisonous draught of self-consumption and self-restraint wore down his frail and ailing body and took his life. It was as if, in despair of the notables, he sought hope in the masses of the people. He held an optimism and a pleasant feeling toward the common, nameless, and unheralded people. He regarded them as beings endowed with an innate nature (fitrat), and in his view human nature was fashioned from goodness and virtue. Perhaps for this reason, he considered the delegation of the decision-making system to the masses of the people in the form of various councils to be the only path to political salvation. In his view, consultation, deliberation, and the council were the foundation of prophetic politics. For this reason, he insisted firmly on the establishment of councils at all levels of political and social life. In considering the masses of the people as endowed with innate nature, perhaps his own inclinations were also involved. Or perhaps, in his definition of human nature, he had allowed one side of the human species' disposition to dominate the other side more than it should. Whatever it was, it seemed far too idealistic for Iranian society. Perhaps Mr. Taleghani needed to read Plato through the eyes of Strauss, or Hobbes's Leviathan.
In any case, he was a human being of unparalleled integrity and, in every respect, immaculate, pure, and great—one of those of whom there should be more in the human world, but there are not. May his lofty and long-suffering soul be in the presence of God's grace and mercy at the highest degree of existence. #احمد_زیدآبادی @ahmadzeidabad

entry.title: [ahmadzeidabad] On the Moscow train, the St. Petersburg to Moscow route was high-speed. Of…
entry.summary:
Machine-translated from the original Telegram post.

Source: @ahmadzeidabad

On the Moscow train, the St. Petersburg to Moscow route was high-speed. Of course, its speed never exceeded 199 kilometers per hour. It covered the roughly 800-kilometer distance between the two cities in exactly 4 hours. The route was entirely flat and forested, covered with young trees. Occasionally, a farm would appear in the middle of the forests. The train passed by several small towns and stopped for only one minute at just two or three intermediate stations. The lush green steppes on both sides of the railway reminded me of a scene from Andrei Tarkovsky's film Mirror—the scene where a beautiful, sorrowful woman sits on the trunk of a dry, fallen tree, waiting for her husband to return from the war front. In that scene, when the wind sweeps through the meadow, it seems as if a glimpse of paradise appears on earth. As it happened, the male voice that informed passengers of the status of intermediate stations sounded like Tarkovsky's voice. The man's voice resonated in my ears like the recitation of a poem, as delicate as the murmur of a gentle autumn rain. I said to myself, how could such a seemingly rough alphabet produce words so fluent, delicate, and sweet? Moscow's air temperature was a few degrees higher than St. Petersburg's, but fortunately, it remained at a mild and pleasant level. Upon exiting the old railway station, Stalin's architectural legacy became evident before our eyes. The massive government buildings, known as the Seven Sisters, dominated central Moscow. They were built by Stalin's order to give grandeur to Moscow. From the very first moment of arriving in the capital, the impatience of its residents compared to those of St. Petersburg was apparent! This impatience manifested itself in the ear-splitting honks of some nervous and hasty drivers in the midday traffic. Our hotel was a skyscraper in what seemed to me a protected spot on the northwestern outskirts of Moscow. The security arrangements inside the hotel were also unexpected. A burly Russian man on the verge of old age, whose cold demeanor and icy gaze were no less than Vladimir Putin's own, monitored the passage of guests and their luggage through the electronic gate in the hotel lobby. He seemed to me like a retired KGB officer! Such visible care and surveillance were clearly linked to the war in Ukraine. In St. Petersburg, apart from a sense of ambiguity and concern in the depths of people's eyes, no other trace or sign of the war was visible. In Moscow, however, the security measures at the hotel and on some of the city's peripheral highways cast a shadow over the capital, however faint, revealing the war's presence. Nevertheless, overall, no sense of war-weariness was visible in the daily lives of the citizens. #احمد_زیدآبادی @ahmadzeidabad
